doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

chapter: Learning jazz and finding Latin music
title: 1976: free jazz, The Untouchables and Studio We
summary: At 15-16 he rejected Latin music, embraced Chick Corea, Stevie Wonder, Oliver Lake and Rashied Ali, played in a free jazz group, was ejected from High School of Music and Art, and learned from older musicians at Studio We.

venues.name: High School of Music and Art

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay. I looked at the year 1976 earlier today wondering what musically was going on. Of course there was a whole lot. In the rock field we had Led Zeppelin was still around and The Ramones. We had disco, Earth, Wind, and Fire. And jazz was Miles of course, “Return to Forever,” Weather Report, Tito Puente was still around. So my question is when you were 16, 15 or 16, what were you choosing from all this music out there plus music at home and at the high school that you were at of Music and Arts. What were you grabbing onto?

Well I was definitely madly in love with “Hymn of the Seventh Galaxy” which is the Chick Corea recording. I must have worn that thing to death. I was also madly in love with “Innervisions” — Stevie Wonder’s “Innervisions.” And I was also madly — I had by the way kind of rejected Latin music as there’s something about being in New York at that period in my school in that neighborhood that made me — it “othered” me, being Latino. It othered me being Mexican, being Cuban. And so I ran as far as I could from that part of my father and mother’s life, and I embraced Oliver Lake, I embraced Rashied Ali, I embraced — so I had a little group I think in 1976 that I was playing with, of musicians, Pablo Calogero and I think some other ones from Marcus Rojas and Heyward Peele and we had a little group called The Untouchables. Sometimes we called ourselves The Untouchables, sometimes we called ourselves The Afroholics. And it was basically a free jazz group oriented kind of — a lot of the stuff that’s very popular now, we were doing back in 1976. And we were playing. We were playing, in fact that’s, you know, kind of — I was so busy playing and making music that I think at that point I’d already been ejected from the High School of Music and Art. At the High School of Music and Art — here’s exactly what happened too – they didn’t have jazz programs, they didn’t have jazz education in those days. The only programs they had were at North Texas State and Berklee, I think UMass were the three programs that taught jazz on any collegiate level. So if you wanted to learn to play jazz, you didn’t get it at the Manhattan School of Music, you didn’t get it — I wasn’t [inaudible] if you wanted to learn to play jazz you had to go hang out with old jazz musicians. And lucky for me there was a place on the Lower East Side called Studio Wee that was run by a man named James DuBois, and musicians, older musicians would go there and hang out all day. People like Sonelius Smith, Jimmy Vass, Clarence Sharp — I mean these were places and they would just hang out all day long just jamming and playing, drinking beer, smoking pot, whatever they did. And we would go. I actually think I got kicked out of high school because I didn’t go to class. I would go down to — I would go to my music classes. I would go to jazz band and theory and musicianship. But most of the time I would make my way down to the Lower East Side and hang out with these old musicians and beg them, beg them for information. “How do you play this chord?
